title: Policy-Based Authorization
description: Implement fine-grained authorization using policies, custom requirements, and handlers to build complex access rules beyond simple role checks.

blocks.text: Roles are great for simple scenarios, but real-world applications often need more nuanced access control. What if only senior employees in the HR department can view salary data? What if a user must have a verified email and be at least 18 years old? Policies let you express these complex rules in code.

Policy-based authorization uses a requirement-handler pattern. A requirement is a simple class that describes what must be true for access to be granted. A handler is a class that evaluates the requirement against the current user's claims and context. Multiple handlers can evaluate the same requirement, and multiple requirements can be combined into a single policy.

blocks.title: The requirement-handler pattern
blocks.text: Think of a requirement as a question: 'Is this user old enough?' The handler is the logic that answers the question by inspecting the user's claims. A policy is a collection of requirements that must all pass for access to be granted.

ASP.NET Core ships with several built-in requirement types that cover common authorization scenarios without requiring custom code. These include role requirements, claim requirements, and authentication scheme requirements.

blocks.title: Built-in policy requirements
items: RequireRole — Requires the user to be in one of the specified roles
RequireClaim — Requires the user to have a specific claim with an optional value
RequireAuthenticatedUser — Requires any authenticated user, equivalent to [Authorize]
RequireAssertion — Inline custom logic using a delegate function
RequireName — Requires the user name to match a specific value

blocks.title: Policies using built-in requirements
blocks.content: Registering policies with role and claim requirements in Program.cs.

blocks.text: In this configuration, 'SeniorHR' requires all three conditions to be true: the user must be in the HR role, have a department claim matching 'Human Resources', and have a years_of_service claim of 5, 10, or 15. All requirements in a policy must pass for access to be granted.

When built-in requirements are not enough, you can create custom requirements and handlers. A requirement is a simple class that implements IAuthorizationRequirement. A handler is a class that inherits from AuthorizationHandler<TRequirement> and contains the evaluation logic.
This pattern is powerful because it separates the authorization rule from where it is used. You can define a MinimumAgeRequirement once and reuse it across multiple policies or controllers.

blocks.title: Custom minimum age requirement and handler
blocks.content: A complete custom requirement and handler that checks if the user meets a minimum age.

blocks.text: The MinimumAgeRequirement class simply holds the minimum age value. The MinimumAgeHandler does the actual work: it finds the DateOfBirth claim, calculates the user's age, and calls context.Succeed(requirement) if the user is old enough. If the claim is missing or the age is too low, the handler does nothing, and the requirement is not met.

After creating the requirement and handler classes, you register the handler in Program.cs and add a policy that uses the requirement. The handler is resolved from the dependency injection container, so you can inject services into the handler's constructor.

blocks.title: Registering the custom handler and policy
blocks.content: Wiring up the MinimumAgeHandler and creating a policy that requires users to be at least 21.

blocks.text: The IAuthorizationHandler interface is registered as scoped so a new handler is created per request. When a user accesses the PurchaseAlcohol action, the authorization system creates a MinimumAgeRequirement with a minimum age of 21, passes it to the MinimumAgeHandler, and grants or denies access based on the result.

Sometimes authorization depends on the specific resource being accessed, not just the user's identity. For example, a user can edit their own posts but not other users' posts. Resource-based authorization lets you make authorization decisions inside your controller or service using IAuthorizationService.

blocks.title: Resource-based authorization for a blog post
blocks.content: Checking if the current user can edit a specific blog post.

blocks.title: Tip: Combine policy and resource authorization
blocks.text: Use [Authorize(Policy)] for broad access rules and IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync for resource-specific checks within your business logic. This gives you defense in depth — a user must pass both the policy and the resource check.

terms.definition: A named set of requirements that must all pass for a user to access a resource.
A marker interface for authorization requirements. A policy can contain multiple requirements.
A class that evaluates an IAuthorizationRequirement and calls context.Succeed() if the user meets it.
Authorization decisions made at runtime based on both the user and the specific resource being accessed.
A service that performs authorization checks programmatically, supporting both policy-based and resource-based checks.

blocks.title: Create a Custom Age Requirement Handler
blocks.description: Build a custom authorization requirement that enforces a minimum age, register it as a policy, and test it with users of different ages.
steps: Create a new ASP.NET Core project with Identity and JWT authentication
Create a MinimumAgeRequirement class implementing IAuthorizationRequirement with a MinimumAge property
Create a MinimumAgeHandler class inheriting from AuthorizationHandler<MinimumAgeRequirement>
In the handler, find the ClaimTypes.DateOfBirth claim, calculate the user's age, and call context.Succeed if age >= MinimumAge
Register the handler with AddScoped<IAuthorizationHandler, MinimumAgeHandler> in Program.cs
Register a policy named 'MustBeAdult' using policy.Requirements.Add(new MinimumAgeRequirement(18))
Create a protected controller action with [Authorize(Policy = "MustBeAdult")]
Test with two users: one with a DateOfBirth claim showing age 25, and one showing age 16 — verify only the 25-year-old can access the endpoint
blocks.expectedOutcome: The endpoint returns 200 OK for the 25-year-old user and 403 Forbidden for the 16-year-old user. The custom handler correctly calculates age from the DateOfBirth claim and enforces the minimum age requirement.

items.hint: Use AddScoped<IAuthorizationHandler, YourHandler>() and add the requirement to a policy.

items.text: I understand resource-based authorization with IAuthorizationService
items.hint: Use AuthorizeAsync(user, resource, policyName) when access depends on the specific resource.

blocks.title: Policy-Based Authorization Summary
points: Policies combine multiple requirements for fine-grained, reusable access rules
Built-in requirements include RequireRole, RequireClaim, and RequireAssertion
Custom requirements implement IAuthorizationRequirement and carry rule data
Custom handlers inherit from AuthorizationHandler<TRequirement> and evaluate the rule
Handlers are registered as scoped services and resolved per request
Resource-based authorization handles access rules that depend on both user and resource
blocks.takeaway: Policy-based authorization is the most powerful and flexible authorization mechanism in ASP.NET Core. It scales from simple role checks to complex business rules while keeping authorization logic centralized and testable.
